- `motifComponent(Class, props)` constructs the class, and the object-form keys (`preconfig`,
  `initializeComponent`, `onMounted`, `childs`, `ref`) apply to it; `motifComponent(fnPart, props)` calls the
  function and applies the same keys to the root it returns: `ref`, the fallthrough attributes (`class`,
  `id`, `aria-*`…), `options`, `transition`, `key` / `indexkey`, `preconfig`, `initializeComponent`, the
  lifecycle hooks and the `x-` keys. The hook and `x-` keys are taken out of the props the function
  receives, as they are kept out of a class's `this.props`; callback props such as `onSave` stay.
  `new Component(fnPart, props)` does the same;
  `motifComponent(instance)` returns the instance as is; `motifComponent({ initializeComponent })` (an
  object with no tag) is a component **without an element**, a fragment: the holder the compiler uses for
  lists. `new Component('div', { initializeComponent })` is the same as the string form and is what the
  test-suite writes.
- `motifFragment({ initializeComponent: (f) => f.controls.add(a, b) })` is a fragment for a branch or a
  slot with several roots (comment markers in the DOM; no attributes, no events on it).
- A third argument (`1`) and the keys `__childExpr`, `__isSvgElement` appear in compiled
  output; they are compiler bookkeeping. Hand-written code leaves them out and never calls
  `motifCompiled` / `_mv`. The `catch (__e) { _mr(__e); … }` around a compiled `{this.part()}`,
  `{a ?? b}` or `{cond && …}` is bookkeeping too (`motifReport` reports the caught error as `MJX208`);
  a hand-written getter needs no `try`/`catch`: the runtime reports its error as `MJX208`.

### `preconfig`

`preconfig: (c) => …` runs when the component is configured, before `onConfig` and before `build()`. A
`bindings.display` / `bindings.wait` registered there keeps an element that starts hidden **unbuilt**
(its subtree, `onBuilt` and `onMounted` wait, like `x-wait` in JSX). The same binding registered in
`initializeComponent` builds the element first and hides it afterwards.

### Text

`'text'` is a real tag: `motifComponent('text', (n) => n.setText('…'))` creates a text node, and text
next to an element is one more child in the same `controls.add` call. The runtime also turns strings and
numbers passed to `controls.add` into text nodes, but the TypeScript signature of `controls.add` takes
components, so TypeScript projects keep a helper:

```ts
import { ComponentBase, motifComponent } from '@motifx/core';
export function text(value: string): ComponentBase {
  return motifComponent('text', (node: ComponentBase) => node.setText(value));
}
```

## Class pages and layouts in a `.ts` file

The Motif Vite plugin also processes `.ts`, `.mts` and `.cts` files: `class Page extends Component<HTMLDivElement>`
gets `static elementTag = 'div'` there as in a `.tsx` file, so the page has its own element. A class that
declares no element type is a **fragment**: `this.class` and `this.attr` have no element to
act on (`this.motif.on` listens on the content elements), and a CSS grid sees the children, not the page. Where the plugin does not process the file (a library
compiled with plain `tsc`), write `static elementTag = 'div'` or call `super('div')`. Two correct shapes:

```ts
// 1. No element declared (the starter's choice): the component is a fragment and view() returns its
//    content. The main below is the first child, not the component's element: this.element is a comment
//    marker; this.class / this.attr and the tag's class / id reach nothing (silently); this.motif.on and
//    the tag's onclick listen on the content elements; x-display and motif.hide() hide the children.
//    Configure main itself.
export default class SettingsPage extends Component {
  settings = this.getService(SettingsService)!;

  override view() {
    return motifComponent('main', (main: ComponentBase) => {
      main.class.add('detail');
      const heading = motifComponent('h1', (h1: ComponentBase) => h1.controls.add(text('Settings')));
      main.controls.add(heading, this.appearance());
    });
  }

  private appearance() { /* returns one component */ }
}

// 2. A declared element; view() then returns the children.
export class Panel extends Component<HTMLDivElement> {
  override onConfigured() { this.class.add('panel'); }
  override view() {
    return motifFragment({ initializeComponent: (f: ComponentBase) => f.controls.add(heading(), body()) });
  }
}
```

The reading order stays the JSX one: children as `const`s, one `controls.add` at the end, and private
methods for the parts (`toolbar(note)`, `editor(note)`), each returning one component. A function part
is a function that returns one component and reads services with `FromService(T)`:

```ts
export function NoteRow(props: { note: Note; folder: Folder }) {
  const nav = useNavigation();
  const { note, folder } = props;
  const open = () => nav.params.id === String(note.id);

  return motifComponent('a', (row: ComponentBase) => {
    row.attr.add({ rel: 'router', href: `/${folder}/${note.id}`, 'aria-current': () => (open() ? 'page' : null) });
    row.class.add(() => `row${open() ? ' active' : ''}`);
    const pin = motifComponent('i', {
      preconfig: (i: ComponentBase) => i.bindings.display(() => note.pinned),
      initializeComponent: (i: ComponentBase) => i.class.add('pin'),
    });
    const title = motifComponent('span', (span: ComponentBase) => span.bindings.text(() => note.title.trim() || 'Untitled'));
    row.controls.add(pin, title);
  });
}
```

A branch of a ternary is a fragment when it has several roots, a component when it has one, and a text
node when it is only text:

```ts
bar.bindings.ternary(
  () => this.state.confirming,
  (frame) => frame.navigate(motifFragment({ initializeComponent: (f) => f.controls.add(question(), confirmButton(), cancelButton()) })),
  (frame) => frame.navigate(this.actions(note)),
);
button.bindings.ternary(() => note.pinned, (f) => f.navigate(text('Pinned')), (f) => f.navigate(text('Pin')));
```

What still works in `.ts`: `@Injectable` and the other decorators (the Vite plugin lowers them in
`.ts` / `.js` files too), DI, the router, `useNavigation()`, transitions, `Virtualization`, and the
`MJX015` check of `motif-lint` (an override that does not reach `super`).

## Porting from JSX or from the docs

`npx motif-explain file.tsx` prints, per expression, the lowered call to write. For a whole file,
`new Compiler().motifCompile(code, 'file.tsx')` from `@motifx/compiler` returns the compiled code; read
it with this key: `_mc` = `motifComponent`, `_mf` = `motifFragment`, `_mfc` = `FNComponent`,
`_mv(1)` = `motifCompiled` (drop it), `_mr(__e)` = `motifReport` (drop it with its `try`/`catch`), `preconfig` = `x-wait` / `x-display`, `indexkey` = `key`,
`__isSvgElement: true` = `options: { isSvg: true }`, `ref: (s) => { this.x = s; if (this.onRefCreated) … }`
= `ref: (s) => (this.x = s)`. Drop `childs: []` and the trailing `, 1`.

## Pitfalls of hand-written views

1. **A fragment by accident.** A class that declares no element type is a fragment, and so is a
   `Component<HTMLDivElement>` class in a file the Motif Vite plugin does not process (a library compiled with
   plain `tsc`); write `static elementTag` or call `super('div')` there. Returning a wrapper from `view()`
   does not give the component an element: it stays a fragment and the wrapper is its first child.
2. **Errors inside `initializeComponent` are swallowed** (`MJX122`, SKILL.md rule 15): the element
   renders empty and `console.error` is the only sign. Typical cause: a `const` that shadows a helper used
   in its own setup (`const text = motifComponent('p', (p) => p.controls.add(text('…')))` calls the
   component, not the helper, when the setup runs at build). `motifComponent` returns `any`, so the type
   checker does not see it. In tests, assert the rendered text or spy on `console.error`.
3. **`display` / `wait` in the wrong hook.** Registered in `initializeComponent` the hidden element is
   built once; register them in `preconfig`.
4. **No compiler, no diagnostics.** `MJX001`–`MJX005`, `MJX016` and the switch/ternary getter rule (SKILL.md rule 6) concern
   JSX only; nothing warns about a `.map()` without `indexkey` or a prop that should be a getter. A plain
   expression in a branch (`motifComponent(Badge, { count: state.n })`) is a snapshot, exactly as in JSX;
   pass `count: () => state.n`.
5. **Types are yours.** Annotate setup parameters (`(c: ComponentBase)`), `ref` targets
   (`search!: Component<HTMLInputElement>`) and `motif.on` handlers (`(_c, e: KeyboardEvent)`).
6. **`controls.add` is immediate** and there is nothing to flush, but reactive *updates* still land on
   a microtask (`await Promise.resolve()` in tests), as in JSX.

---

<!-- references/jsx-and-reactivity.md -->

# JSX, reactivity and bindings

## Reactive primitives (`@motifx/core` exports)

Each tool is for a different shape of state; pick by what is held. `reactive` for a model with fields
(nested objects, arrays, `Map`/`Set`; every field tracked on its own; the usual component and service
state). `createSignal` for one value (a selected id, a scroll offset): written whole, an in-place change
of an object inside it needs `mutate()`, equality can be customised. `createComputed` for a derived value
that is read all the time, `createLazyComputed` for an expensive one read less often than its inputs
change. `effect` (in a component `bindings.watch`) for side effects. They share one tracking system, read
each other and reach the DOM through the same bindings.

```ts
import { reactive, useModel, createSignal, createComputed, createLazyComputed, createSelection, asReadonly, isReadonly, effect, untracked, deepClone, clearModel, read, toGetter } from '@motifx/core';
```

| API | Notes |
|---|---|
| `reactive(obj)` / `useModel(obj)` | Deep proxy over the object itself (no copy). Read = tracked, write = triggers. A write that leaves the value unchanged (`Object.is`) wakes no reader, on array indices and `length` too; a reactive object written into a reactive field or array is stored raw and read back reactive. Nested objects and arrays (`push`, `splice`, sort, index assignment, `length = 0`) are tracked, and so are `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet` (see Reactive collections). The same object gives the same proxy and a proxy passed in is returned as is, until `clearModel(obj)` drops the entry (then `reactive(obj)` gives a new proxy). A number, string or boolean is boxed: `reactive('')` returns a `{ value: '' }` proxy, typed `{ value: T }`. Component, `Application` and `ServiceProvider` instances and `app.router` are returned as is, also when stored in a reactive field. `Date`, `RegExp` and non-extensible (frozen, sealed) objects are returned as is, never proxied. A `RegExp` works normally inside a reactive object (`test`, `exec`, `replace`); a new pattern is written as a new `RegExp` to the field, which triggers. `Date` and frozen objects are not tracked inside (write a new reference). Getters and methods called through the proxy get the proxy as `this`, so a class whose getter or method touches a `#private` field throws `TypeError` once wrapped, directly or as a value inside a reactive object; keep that class's reactive state in a `reactive({ … })` field instead (a TypeScript `private` field is an ordinary field and works). A function-valued field is returned as the function itself; a binding that ends up with a function value calls it: `{state.fn}`, `bindings.add(prop, state, 'fn')` and attribute getters call it unbound (no `this`), `x-text={state.fn}` calls it on `state`. A method that uses `this` goes into a slot as `{() => state.fn()}`, and your own code must call it: `() => state.fn() + '!'`. |
| `createSignal(v)` / `new Signal(v, equals?)` / `Signal.create(v, equals?)` | `.value` get/set (a write that `equals`, default `Object.is`, finds equal triggers nothing), `.peek()`, `.update(fn)`, `.mutate(fn)` and `.notify()` (both trigger even when the reference is unchanged), `.asReadonly()` (`value`, `peek()`), `.dispose()` (writes become no-ops, reads return the last value), `valueOf()` / `toString()` (tracked reads, so `` `${sig}` `` is tracked). |
| `createComputed(fn)` | Eager, cached derived value: computed at creation; on a dependency change it recomputes on the next microtask even when unread, and wakes its readers only when the value changed. `.value` returns the cached value without computing, so a synchronous read right after a write gives the previous value. Writes in one synchronous block cost one recomputation. `.value`, `.peek()`, `.dispose()` (stops recomputing, keeps the last value). |
| `createLazyComputed(fn)` | Lazy derived value: nothing is computed until `.value` is read; a dependency change only marks it dirty (synchronously) and wakes its readers, even when the value will turn out equal; any number of writes between two reads costs one computation. `.value`, `.peek()` (computes when dirty, untracked), `.isDirty`, `.dispose()` (stops tracking; a dirty value is computed once more on the next read, then the last value is returned). With a `createComputed` in the chain the lazy value is fresh only after the flush. Choose `createComputed` for a value read all the time, `createLazyComputed` for an expensive value read less often than it is written. |
| `createSelection(fn)` | Keyed selection: returns `isSelected(key)`. Inside a binding or effect it subscribes only to that key, so when the source changes only the bindings of the previous and the new value run again: write `class={{ 'is-selected': () => isSelected(note.id) }}` instead of `() => state.selected === note.id` on every row (a 60 000-row list selects in 0.2 ms instead of 49). Keys are compared with `Object.is` after unwrapping reactive objects; outside an effect it only compares; equality only (a `>` comparison cannot be keyed, keep a plain getter); `isSelected.dispose()` stops following the source. Type `KeySelection<T>`. |
| `asReadonly(obj)` / `isReadonly(v)` | Live read-only view of a reactive object, array, `Map` or `Set`, not a copy: reads are tracked and follow every change made through the reactive object, and what it hands out (nested objects, items, map values, set elements) is read-only too. Writing, deleting, a mutating array method (`push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`, …) and `Map`/`Set` changes throw `MJX212` in strict and sloppy code alike; the data does not change. One object, one view; `reactive(view)` returns the view, so no writable proxy can be had from it. Type `DeepReadonly<T>`. `isReadonly` is true only for such views; a frozen object is returned as is. Hand a service's state to components this way while changes go through the service's methods. |
| `effect(fn, onValueChanged?)` | Runs immediately and again on every change of what it read. `onValueChanged(value)` receives `fn`'s return value after every run, outside `fn`'s tracking; `value` is typed from `fn`'s return type. If `fn` throws, `onValueChanged` is not called for that run (`MJX208` is reported, tracking continues). The first `onValueChanged` call runs synchronously inside `effect(...)`; when the effect is created while another effect is running, the reads of that first call are recorded on the outer effect. Returns `stop()`. Inside components prefer `this.bindings.watch(fn)`. |
| `untracked(fn)` | Reads inside are not tracked by the enclosing effect; writes inside still trigger their readers; returns `fn`'s value. Nested `effect()` calls still track normally. |
| `deepClone(v)` | Non-reactive deep copy of the raw value: plain objects (own enumerable keys), arrays, `Map` and `Set` are copied deeply; `Date` and `RegExp` become new instances; a class instance keeps its prototype, so its getters and methods work on the copy; cycles are reproduced; functions, `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` are shared; DOM nodes are copied with `cloneNode(true)`; boxed primitives become primitives. |
| `clearModel(m)` | Drops the proxy entries of the object and of its already proxied nested objects; values, bindings and effects stay. Afterwards `reactive(m)` gives a new proxy, and writes through it still update the existing bindings. Writes through a proxy taken before the call change the value without notifying; nested objects read from that old proxy come out as new proxies that do notify. |
| `read(v)` / `toGetter(v)` | `Bind<T>` is `T \| (() => T)`: `read` calls a function and returns anything else as is, `toGetter` always returns a getter. The contract for props that may arrive as getters (see the ternary rule under Attributes). |
| `configureReactivityLeakMonitor({ enabled?, threshold?, name? })` | Dev leak monitor: warns `MJX507` when the number of effects tracking one field reaches `threshold` (200 by default when enabled); `app.useReactiveMonitor(...)` is the same switch. |
| `asyncTracking` | `capture()`/`suspend()`/`resume()`/`end()`; emitted by the compiler around each `await` of an `async` function written inline on `<Virtualization dataRequest={…}>`, so reads after `await` stay tracked. A function passed by name (`dataRequest={this.loadPage}`) or one that is not `async` is not wrapped, and its reads after `await` are not tracked. Not needed in app code. |

Effects flush on a microtask in rounds; writes in one synchronous block run each queued effect once. An
effect that also reads a value written in the same flush by another effect or by a `createComputed` runs
again in the next round of that microtask: depending on creation order its first run may see the old value,
its last run sees the current ones, and the final state does not depend on creation order. An effect that
runs 50 times in one flush (it writes what it reads, e.g. `state.n++`) is skipped for the rest of that flush
and raises the `MJX203` dev warning; wrap the write in `untracked(...)`. An effect that tracks more than 1000
dependencies in one run raises `MJX209` once (owner named when devtools are on): it is scanning a reactive list;
look items up by key or read the list with `untracked(...)`; `useReactiveMonitor({ dependencies })` sets the limit.
`MJX210` fires once per list when two or more instances of one component (eight owner-less effects) scan the same reactive
list with `find`/`findIndex`/`findLast`/`findLastIndex`/`some`/`every` and the list has at least as many items as there are
scanners, wherever the list came from (props, another module, a service); a three-item settings list read by a hundred
rows stays quiet, and the check needs devtools on (`useDevelopment(true)`); `useReactiveMonitor({ scans: false })` switches it off.

Module-level stores are idiomatic:

```ts
// store/session.ts
export const session = reactive({ user: null as User | null, theme: 'light' });
```

### Reactive collections

`Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` inside a reactive model (or passed to `reactive()` directly) are
reactive; mutate them in place, no need to replace the whole collection.

```tsx
const state = reactive({ users: new Map<string, User>(), selected: new Set<string>() });
state.users.set(u.id, u);
state.selected.add(u.id);
state.users.get(u.id)!.name = 'Grace';           // values read out are reactive proxies
<ul>{[...state.users.values()].map(u =>
  <li key={u.id} class={state.selected.has(u.id) ? 'selected' : ''}>{u.name}</li>)}</ul>
```

- `get(k)` / `has(k)` rerun only when that key changes; `size`, `forEach`, `values()`, `entries()`,
  `for…of` and spread rerun on any content change; `Map.keys()` reruns only when a key is added or removed.
- No-op writes trigger nothing: `set` with an `Object.is`-equal value, `add` of a present element,
  `delete` of a missing key, `clear` on an empty collection.
- `Map` values and `Set` elements come out as reactive proxies; `Map` keys come out raw. Proxies written
  in are stored raw, and object keys match whether given raw or reactive.
- Identity, `instanceof`, chaining and `Object.prototype.toString` behave natively; `WeakMap`/`WeakSet`
  expose only their own methods.

## Expression forms inside JSX

| You write | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `{"text"}` | Static. |
| `{localVar}` | Guarded getter `bindings.add('textContent', () => …)`: a string/number local is written once (nothing reactive is read); a local holding a function is called inside the binding and stays live; `null`/`undefined` gives empty text; a component (or array of them) is placed with `controls.add`. |
| `{fn()}` | Plain call: `controls.add(fn())`, evaluated once; the one-shot form. |
| `{state.field}` | One-way binding to that field (`bindings.add('textContent', state, 'field')`). Only the last field is tracked; the object before it is read once at setup, so `{editor.selected.title}` follows that note's title but stays on the old note when `editor.selected` changes; `{() => editor.selected?.title}` tracks the whole path. A path with `?.` is wrapped in a getter and stays live. |
| `{() => expr}` | Reactive getter; re-evaluated when any reactive read inside changes. Most flexible. |
| `` {`Count: ${state.n}`} `` | Template literal is wrapped in a getter → reactive. |
| `{cond && <X/>}` | Conditional (bindings.when) — **constructs and disposes on every toggle**; rebuilt only when the condition value changes. Prefer `x-wait` (see below). |
| `{a ?? b}` / `{a \|\| b}` | Left when present (`??`: not null/undefined; `\|\|`: truthy), else right; reactive; right may be JSX (bindings.method). |
| `{this.method(x)}` | Member call: a returned component is inserted (Frame, re-evaluated on reactive change), a string becomes reactive text (bindings.method). |
| `{cond ? <A/> : <B/>}` | Two-branch (bindings.ternary), nested ternaries allowed; a branch is rebuilt only when its condition value changes. |
| `{arr.map(item => <li key={item.id}/>)}` | List (bindings.list); rows matched by the item object. `.filter().map()`, `[x].map()` and `(c ? xs : ys).map()` work. |
| `{this.childs}` / `{[compA, compB]}` | Insert component instances. |
| `{someComponentInstance}` | Insert. |

A getter that returns JSX (`{() => cond ? <A/> : <B/>}`) is also supported and behaves like a
reactive single-content slot.

## Attributes

```tsx
<input type="text" placeholder="Search" />         // static
<a href={state.url} />                              // reactive field
<img src={() => state.avatar} />                    // reactive getter
<button disabled={() => state.busy}>Go</button>
<input value={() => state.q} oninput={(e) => state.q = e.target.value} />
<label for="email" />                               // `for` is fine (not htmlFor)
```

Rule: **a function value = reactive binding; anything else = set once.** On a plain DOM tag the
compiler wraps an expression that reads a variable (`a + b`, `!state.open`, `state.url`, a template literal,
a `?.` chain) in a getter,
so it stays live; a plain call (`data-n={fmt(x)}`) is evaluated once; a bare identifier (`attr={v}`) is
passed as is (live only when it holds a function); literal values (numbers, negative
numbers, `true`/`false`, `null`, arrays, `new X()`) are passed to `attr.add` as they are. `action` and
`formaction` are the exception where the resolved **value** may be a function: it is bound as the
submit handler instead of being written as the URL (see `events-and-forms.md`).

Attribute values: `false`, `null` and `undefined` remove the attribute, `true` and a valueless attribute
(`<button disabled />`) write `""`, strings and numbers are written as they are (`tabindex={0}` →
`"0"`). On `aria-*` and `data-*` a boolean is written as text: `aria-expanded={false}` →
`aria-expanded="false"`, `data-on={true}` → `"true"`; `null`/`undefined` still remove it. `attr.add({ title: null, role: 'tab' })` removes `title` and still writes `role`.

Attribute names are only the own keys of the object given to `attr.add`; a value is never traversed.
An object or array value is written as one attribute value, converted to text: `title={obj}` →
`title="[object Object]"`, `data-ids={[1, 2]}` → `data-ids="1,2"`, and a getter returning an object or
array writes the same text. On a method-like prop the value is the argument instead (see
[Method-like props](#method-like-props)).

**Security:** attributes written on the tag and `attr.add` values are written without filtering. When a
URL attribute (`href`, `src`, `action`, `formaction`) is bound to user data, a `javascript:` value runs
code on click, so validate the scheme first, e.g.
`href={() => /^(https?:|mailto:|\/|#|\.)/i.test(u.trim()) ? u : '#'}`. `attr.add({ innerHTML })` writes
HTML as is, like `x-html`. Only a spread drops `innerHTML`, `srcdoc` and `javascript:` URLs on its own.

**One deliberate exception: a ternary in attribute/prop position is always wrapped lazily** —
`mode={x ? 'a' : 'b'}` compiles to `mode: () => x ? 'a' : 'b'`, on DOM tags and component tags alike,
so the expression stays reactive instead of freezing at `view()` time. The contract for the receiving
component is to declare that prop as `Bind<T>` and read it with `read()` / `toGetter()` (all three exported from `@motifx/core`); a component
that declares a plain type and passes the prop straight through gets a function at runtime (e.g. an
`Icon` that looks up `name` directly receives `() => …` from `<Icon name={ok ? 'check' : 'error'}/>`).
A valueless attribute on a component tag (`<Comp flag />`) passes `flag: true`. `npx motif-lint`
flags a ternary on a prop whose declared type is not `Bind<T>` (`MJX005`). On a component tag the other
expressions are not wrapped (`{p.a}`, `{f()}`, `{a && b}` pass the value taken at setup), while on a plain
DOM tag `{p.a}` and `{a && b}` are wrapped and `{f()}` runs once. A ternary in a handler position
(`onclick={a ? save : edit}`, `on:click`, `onclick:once`, also on a component tag) is wrapped too, but nothing
calls the handler it returns: the getter becomes the listener, a click only returns the chosen handler, and no
warning appears. Put the condition inside the handler: `onclick={() => (a ? save() : edit())}`.

**When in doubt, do not guess the lowering — print it.** `npx motif-explain file.tsx` lists every
JSX expression with the real generated call (`sender.bindings.add("textContent", state, "ad")`,
`sender.bindings.when(…)`, `sender.attr.add({ title: () => … })`…), its reactivity class and its
dependency surface. JSX here is shorthand for the binding API; the compiler is a lowering pass, and
`explain` is its `-S` flag.

### Children: conditionals and prebuilt components

**Prefer the `x-wait` directive over `{cond && <X/>}`.** `<X x-wait={() => !cond} />` waits while the
function returns `true`: if it is `true` initially the element is never built (subtree included), and
toggling it later only hides/shows — the instance and its state survive. `{cond && <X/>}` instead
builds a fresh instance on every show and disposes it on every hide. Use `&&` only when that dispose
is what you want. Full comparison in `references/conditionals-lists-frames.md`.

`&&` and ternary branches are rebuilt only when the condition **value** changes (`Object.is`; for
`&&` two falsy values count as the same); while it stays the same the branch keeps its component
instance and state. A component prop written as a plain expression inside a branch
(`<Badge count={state.n}/>`) is therefore a snapshot taken when the branch was built, exactly as
outside a conditional. Pass a getter (`count={() => state.n}`) and read it on the receiving side with
the `Bind<T>` / `read()` / `toGetter()` contract to keep it live.

`{cond && <X/>}` uses **JS truthiness** — `false`, `null`, `undefined`, `0`, `''` render nothing — both
inside a real element and at a fragment (`<>…</>`) root.

**Component-valued props need no special syntax.** `{props.headerTemplate}`, `{this.props.tpl}`,
`{parts}`, `{one}` holding a component (or an array of them) are placed into `controls` instead of
being stringified; non-component values keep the reactive text binding. So a slot prop and a data prop
are written the same way:

```tsx
<div>{props.headerTemplate}{props.title}</div>   // component slot + reactive text
<Card headerTemplate={<h1>Title</h1>} title="Sub" />
```

The braces may be left out: `headerTemplate=<h1>Title</h1>` compiles exactly like `headerTemplate={<h1>Title</h1>}`.

The decision is made **once, when the parent's `initializeComponent` places it**: the placed component's own bindings stay live,
but reassigning the prop later does not swap the DOM. Props are a plain object taken when the tag is set up,
so `{() => props.headerTemplate}` does not track a later assignment either (nothing reactive is read inside).
**If the template can change (starts `null`, gets swapped at runtime)**, the parent passes it through a
ternary or a getter (`headerTemplate={state.editing ? <nav/> : null}`; a prop ternary is always a getter),
and the child declares the prop `Bind<ComponentBase | null>` and reads it inside a getter with `read()`:
`{() => read(props.headerTemplate)}` creates a `Frame` slot and places the current result on every change. If a component reaches a text binding anyway, nothing is written
and an `MJX204` dev warning names the getter fix.

### Spread `{...props}`

On a **plain DOM tag** the spread object is applied as if the attributes were written inline:
`class`/`className` → `class.add` (merged with an inline `class`), `style` → `style()`, `value`/`checked`/
`selected` → property binding, `on*` (`onclick`, `onClick`, `oninput:once`) → DOM listener, everything else
→ attribute. Getters stay live; functions that take parameters (`renderItem: (x) => …`) are skipped.
Inline attributes are applied after the spread, so `<div {...p} id="fixed"/>` keeps `id="fixed"`, even when
`p.id` is a getter: the inline write owns the attribute and the getter stops writing it (the spread's other
getters stay live). The same rule holds for `attr.add`: the last `attr.add` for a key owns that key. It holds for
`value`/`checked`/`selected` as well (a later `bindings.add('value', …)` replaces the earlier binding; the `x-model`
binding is not replaced) and per key for `style`: an inline `style={{ color: 'blue' }}` takes only `color` from a spread
style getter, whose other keys stay live, and an inline style string takes the whole attribute.
A spread never sets `innerHTML` or `srcdoc` (dev warning `MJX124`) and never writes a `javascript:` URL to `href`/`src`/
`action`/`formaction`/`xlink:href` (dev warning `MJX125`; a getter's current value is removed). Use `x-html` (or inline `srcdoc`) for
trusted HTML and write an intended `javascript:` link inline on the tag; inline attributes are not filtered.

On a **component tag** (`<Card {...props}/>`, `<Card class="x" id="y"/>`) only the **common attributes**
fall through to the component's own element (attribute fallthrough): `class`/`className` (merged
with the component's own classes), `style`, `id`, `tabindex`, `role`, `aria-*`, `data-*`. Getters
stay live. Data/callback props (`items`, `label`, `onSave`, `disabled`) are never written to the root, and
neither is `title` — deliberately, since it is a very common data prop name (`<Card title="…"/>`).
Everything, including the fallen-through keys, remains readable in `this.props`. The types accept these
keys and DOM event props on every component tag (even with a custom constructor props type); a prop the
component declares under the same name keeps its own type. The component's own
`onConfigured`/`initializeComponent` attributes win for the same attribute (fallthrough is applied in the constructor).
Function components behave the same: the tag's common attributes land on the returned root (no double
application when the root is `<div {...props}/>`). A component without an element (a fragment: a class that
declares none, an Options object with `el: undefined`/`null`) silently ignores them, and DOM event props on
its tag listen on its content elements. An Options object whose `el` is a ready DOM node is a component root exactly like
`el: 'div'`: the same common attributes fall through and nothing else is written to the node.

### `class` / `className`

String, array, object map or getter: `class={() => ({ active: state.on, big: size > 2 })}`.

In an object written in JSX the key is the class name and the value is its condition: the class is added
while the value is truthy and removed otherwise. Literals (`true`, `false`, `''`, `0`, `null`) apply once; any
other value is wrapped in a getter and stays live, inside an array too:
`class={{ row: true, danger: state.sel === id }}`, `class={['card', { active: () => state.on }]}`.

On a component tag only a ternary is wrapped: an object, a template literal or `class={note.cls}` is
evaluated once when the tag is set up and applied to the component's element with `class.add`; pass
`{ selected: () => note.pinned }` or `class={() => …}` for a live class there. The tag's `class` is applied in
the constructor and the component's own classes later, so `<NoteBadge class="small" />` whose `onConfigured`
adds `badge` renders `class="small badge"`.

### `style`

String, object (`{ width: '33%' }`) or getter returning either. A getter is **live**: keys it stops
returning are cleared; a returned string replaces the whole inline style. `this.style(fn)` keeps one
watcher — calling it again stops the previous one. An object written after the getter (`style({ color: 'blue' })`)
takes those keys from it; a string written after the getter stops it. CSS custom properties (`{ '--accent': c }`)
are written like any other key, in objects and getters; a `null` or `''` value removes one.

### Method-like props

On a **plain DOM tag**, props named after element methods call the method instead of writing an
attribute. A getter or reactive field re-applies on every change (`showModal={() => state.open}`);
the call runs one microtask later. On a component tag these names are ordinary props.

- `focus`: only strict `false` → `blur()`; an object → `focus(options)` (`focus={{ preventScroll: true }}`);
  every other value (`true`, `undefined`, `null`, `0`, `''`) → `focus()` with no argument. `focus={() => f.editing}` with `editing` starting `undefined`
  therefore calls `focus()` on the first run; start the field at `false`.
- `show`, `showModal` / `showPopover`: truthy → call, `false` → `close()` / `hidePopover()`.
- `togglePopover`: boolean → `togglePopover(bool)`, other truthy → `togglePopover()`.
- `play` (falsy → `pause()`), `select` (falsy → clears the selection), `requestFullscreen` /
  `requestPointerLock` (falsy → exit): truthy → call.
- `close`, `hidePopover`, `requestSubmit`, `checkValidity`, `reportValidity`, `showPicker`, `load`:
  `true` → `method()`, other truthy → `method(value)` (`close={() => 'cancel'}`); falsy → nothing.
- `blur`, `click`, `pause`, `submit`, `reset`, `exitFullscreen`, `exitPointerLock`,
  `requestPictureInPicture`, `exitPictureInPicture`: truthy → call; falsy → nothing. The three `exit*`
  methods are called on `document`, not on the element.
- `scrollIntoView`: `true`/`null`/`undefined` → `scrollIntoView()`, anything else (including `false`) → `scrollIntoView(value)`.
- `scrollTo`, `scrollBy`: only an object or array → `method(value)`.
- `setSelectionRange`, `setRangeText`, `setPointerCapture`, `releasePointerCapture`, `fastSeek`:
  any value except `null`/`undefined`/`false` → `method(value)`.

An array value is spread into arguments (`setSelectionRange={[0, 5]}` or `setSelectionRange={() => [0, 5]}`
→ `setSelectionRange(0, 5)`); an object value is passed as one argument (`scrollTo={{ top: 0 }}`).
Literal values call the method too: `showModal={true}`, `focus={true}`, and a valueless `<dialog show />`
counts as `true`. Only the names listed here are called: any other name, also one that is an element method
(`setCustomValidity`, `stepUp` …), is written as a plain attribute, and so is a listed name the element does
not have.

### Special `x-` props

| Prop | Effect |
|---|---|
| `ref={(s) => ...}` / `ref={this.x}` / `x-ref` | Capture the tag's component instance (callback, or a member/name that is called when it is a function and assigned otherwise; every tag, exactly once). `ref` and `x-ref` on one tag both run, in source order. Applied only to the component it was given to (a function component's returned root); never present in `props` / `this.props`, so `{...props}` does not forward it. Use a separately named prop (`inputRef`) for an inner element. |
| `x-html={() => html}` | Reactive `innerHTML` (unsafe with untrusted input). |
| `x-text`, `x-value`, `x-watch`, `x-model` | Compile to `sender.bindings.text(…)` / `.value(…)` / `.watch(…)` / `.model(…)`. `x-text` sets the element's whole `textContent`: on its first change it removes the element's other children, so write `{() => text}` as a child for live text next to siblings. `x-model={() => s.q}` (or `x-model={s.q}`) becomes `bindings.model(() => s.q, v => { s.q = v })`: two-way, and the owner object is read again on every write. A value that is not a member access binds one-way (events-and-forms.md). |
| `x-inject={v}` | Passed as the prop `inject` (no attribute on a plain DOM tag). |
| `x-foo` (unknown) | Passed as the prop `onfoo`; compiler warning `MJX007`. `x-bind`, `x-focus`, `x-list`, `x-loop`, `x-effect`, `x-reload`, `x-interrupt`, `x-to` are compile errors (`MJX006`). |
| `x-wait={() => bool}` | While `true`, the component is held back from the DOM. |
| `x-display={() => bool}` | Show/hide (uses `hideStrategy`). |
| `x-chunk` / `x-chunk={50}` | Builds the element's children in slices: the first 100 added together (or exactly n with a number) build at once, the rest leave a `<!--h-->` trace and build in order over the next frames, as many per frame as keep the frame near 50 ms (at least n with a number); `.map` rows under it are created only on their turn, with the index they have then. No value or a number; a string, object or arrow function stops the build with `MJX012`. `options: { chunk: true }` or `options: { chunk: 50 }` in code. |
| `x-style={...}` | Same as `style` (compiles to `sender.style(...)`; getter live). |
| `x-config`, `x-configured`, `x-building`, `x-built`, `x-mounted`, `x-activated`, `x-deactivated`, `x-disposing`, `x-disposed`, `x-initializing`, `x-initialized`, `x-visibilitychanged` (or `x:config`…, `onConfig`, `onBuilt`, `onMounted`, …) | Lifecycle hooks as props. Several spellings of one hook on the same tag (`onBuilt` + `x-built` + `x:built`) are merged: all of them run once, in source order. On a function component tag every spelling reaches the returned root; `initializing`/`initialized` fire right after the root is constructed, in the class tag order (`ref` → `initializing` → `initialized` → `config`). |
| `key` | Identifies a list item; duplicates raise the `MJX202` dev warning. Rows are matched by the item object, so `key` does not change DOM reuse. |
| `transition="fade"` or `transition={{...}}` | Enter/leave CSS classes (styling-and-transitions.md). No attribute is written, also on plain DOM tags. |
| `options={{ hideStrategy, disableDisposal }}` | Copied into the tag's `motif.options` (plain DOM tags and component tags); no attribute is written. |
| `initializeComponent={(s) => ...}` | Called once with the tag's component as `sender`, during build right before `view()` (a tag held by `x-wait` runs it on its first show); good place for `s.bindings.*` calls. Same meaning and timing on plain DOM tags, class component tags and function component tags (the returned root). The compiler emits its own `initializeComponent` for the tag's attributes, events, directives and children; both run: the component's method, then the tag's, then the compiled one. With JSX you rarely write it; it is mainly for building components without JSX. |

On every directive but `x-chunk` (`x-wait`/`x-display` included) a variable or member holding a function is called as the
getter, with `this` for a method: `x-display={isAuthor}`, `x-wait={this.isLoading}`, `x-text={this.label}`.
`x-chunk` (and `options: { chunk }`) calls such a function once, when the component is set up, and uses the value it returns;
later changes are not tracked.

## The bindings API (`this.bindings` / `sender.bindings`)

The compiler generates these; you can call them directly in `initializeComponent`/`onConfig` or in tests.

```ts
add(prop, source)                        // bind DOM property `prop` to reactive object/getter
add(prop, source, member)                // bind to source[member]; member may be a dotted path ('author.name')
add(prop, source, member, formatString)
add(prop, source, member, formatString, formatInfo)   // formatInfo: { locale?, currency? }
add(binding)                             // an object with `propertyName` is registered as is
text(() => string)                       // textContent
value(() => any)                         // value
html(() => string)                       // innerHTML
when(() => cond, () => component)        // conditional; rebuilt when the cond value changes (Object.is, falsy values equal)
ternary(() => cond, frame => frame.navigate(A), frame => frame.navigate(B))   // branch rebuilt when the cond value changes
list(() => items, (item, i) => component) // rows matched by item object identity, not by key
loop(...)                                // alias of list
switchCase(() => key, { a: frame => ..., b: frame => ... }, frame => defaultCase)
method(() => any)                        // string/number/boolean/bigint → text; component → Frame slot;
                                         // null/undefined in slot mode empties it (old component disposed)
watch(() => void)                        // side-effect; first run synchronously at registration; auto-stopped on dispose
model(getter, setter)                    // two-way through functions; what `x-model` compiles to
model(source, member, format?, formatInfo?) // two-way (checked/value/src chosen by element type)
model(binding)                           // any single object argument is taken as an IBaseBinding;
                                         // a single function argument binds one-way (no write-back)
writeModel(value)                        // write back through this component's model/x-model bindings; false if none
wait(() => bool); display(() => bool)
remove(binding); clear()                 // deactivate registered bindings
activateAll(); deactivateAll()           // deactivateAll also empties the registry
reActivateAll()                          // see "Non-reactive data"
items                                    // copy of the registered bindings
```

`add`, `html`, `list`/`loop`, `model`, `wait`, `display` register a binding and return it; `text` and
`value` register one and return nothing. `clear` (and `remove` with the returned binding) stops them. `when`, `ternary` and `switchCase` return `null`, `method` and `watch`
return nothing; none of them is registered, so `remove`/`clear` cannot stop them, while `reActivateAll()` restarts them. All five stop when the
component is disposed; the inner condition of a nested ternary also stops when the outer branch switches away.

A `Binding` (returned by `add`/`model`) has `converter` (applied to the value read, after
`formatString`), `converterBack` (applied to the DOM value before `model` writes it back), `setter`
(the write function of the getter/setter form) and `formatInfo`; set them on the returned binding before
the component is built. `updateMode` is not read by any binding.

Registered bindings start with the component: `add` (and the other registering calls) activates the binding at
once only when the component is already built; otherwise `build()` activates it. A value needed before the build
is read once by hand.

Where `add(prop, source)` writes the value, in this order: `'wait'` / `'display'` → `isWait`; `'text'` /
`'textContent'` → `setText()` (replaces the element's whole `textContent`); `'html'` / `'innerHTML'` →
`innerHTML`; `'visible'` / `'visibility'` → `motif.show()` / `motif.hide()`; `'style'` → `style()` (object values
only); `'model'` → the input's `value` or `checked`. Any other name: `'value'` goes to `component.value` when the
component has one; else a name the element has (`tabIndex`, `title`, `hidden`, `disabled`, `placeholder`…) is
set on the element directly; else a name the component has is assigned to it (`component[name] = value`, its
setter or field). A name found nowhere writes nothing. A dotted name is a path on the component and starts
there, skipping the special names and the element: `add('options.locked', fn)` writes
`component.options.locked`, calling a setter on the way; nothing is written when a step is missing or is not an
object. Before writing, a value that is a function is called with
no arguments, again while the result is still a function, so a function held in the source (a formatter, a
check) is never written as it is.

So a component can bind its own property, and that is how a component follows a prop given as a function: it
binds the prop to its own setter. Reactive data re-runs the binding by itself; with plain data the owner calls
`setState()` / `reState()` and the binding reads the prop again. A plain value prop is written once.

```tsx
class NoteBody extends Component<HTMLDivElement, { note: Note; locked: Bind<boolean> }> {
  get locked() { return this.class.has('locked'); }
  set locked(value: boolean) { if (value) this.class.add('locked'); else this.class.remove('locked'); }
  onConfigured() { this.bindings.add('locked', this.props.locked); }   // value or getter
  view() { return <p>{this.props.note.body}</p>; }
}
// <NoteBody note={note} locked={() => note.archived} />; plain note: change it, then page.reState()
```

An Options object can declare the same `get`/`set` pair (it is copied onto the component) and call
`this.bindings.add('locked', props.locked)` in `onConfigured`. A function component has no property of its
own: it follows the prop with `bindings.watch` on its root
(`onBuilt={(c) => c.bindings.watch(() => …read(props.locked)…)}`), which `setState()` / `reState()` re-run too.
Limits of a property binding:

- A name the element also has (`title`, `hidden`, `disabled`, `tabIndex`…) is written to the element, never to
  the component.
- A method name is overwritten by the value, not called; call the method from `bindings.watch` or make the
  property a setter.
- A function value is called before writing, so a function-valued property (a formatter, a comparer) is assigned
  directly, not bound.
- A value written from code is replaced on the binding's next run (a reactive change, `setState()`, `reState()`);
  `bindings.remove(binding)` (the binding `add` returned) hands the property to code.

`add(binding)` registers your own binding object: anything with `propertyName`, `dataSource`, `activate()`,
`deactivate()` and `reActivate()` (the `IBaseBinding` shape; the type is not exported and the object is matched
by shape). It joins the same registry, so `setState()` / `reState()` call its `reActivate()`, `remove(binding)`
and `clear()` call its `deactivate()`, and so does disposing the component. Without an optional `pause()`
method, the pause before a dispose calls `deactivate()` too, so it can run twice and must be safe to repeat.
`reActivate()` re-reads and writes again without tearing anything down. The object decides where the value
goes, so it can follow a getter in an effect and write the result to a component's own field instead of a public
setter; nothing calls the value for it.

`formatString` codes: on numbers `C` → currency, `P` → percent (the value is multiplied by 100: `0.25` →
`25%`), `N`/`N2` → fixed decimals (default 2), the number codes also in lower case;
on `Date` values `d` → `toLocaleDateString`, `t` → `toLocaleTimeString`; any other value is written
with `toString()`. `null`/`undefined` are not formatted. Locale and currency come from the binding's
`formatInfo` (`{ locale?: string | string[], currency?: string }`):
`bindings.add('textContent', s, 'price', 'C', { locale: 'en-US', currency: 'USD' })` → `$1,234.50`.
Without `locale` the runtime's default locale applies (the `Intl` default); without `currency`, `C`
writes the amount with two decimals and no currency symbol.

Example without JSX (as used in the test-suite):

```ts
const data = reactive({ message: 'Hello' });
const c = new Component('div', { initializeComponent: (s) => { s.bindings.text(() => data.message); } });
c.build();
document.body.appendChild(c.element);
data.message = 'World'; // textContent updates after a microtask
```

## Non-reactive data

Prefer reactive data (`reactive(obj)`). For plain objects mutated in place, `this.setState()` refreshes
the subtree: it calls `setState()` on each child, then `bindings.reActivateAll()`, which re-runs every
registered binding of the component (text and attribute paths, class and style getters, `x-text`, `x-html`,
`value`/`checked`/`x-model`, `wait`/`display`; each list matches its rows to the items again like a
reactive update: a kept item keeps its row, a new item gets one row, a removed item's row is disposed) and restarts
`when`, `ternary`, `switchCase`, `method` (`{() => …}`, template literals, member calls) and `watch`. A
branch is rebuilt only when its condition value changed. `reState()` does the same with this component
first, then its children. A path written directly (`{i18n.dict.title}`, `bindings.add('textContent', dict,
'title')`) keeps the object it read at build time, so replacing that object leaves the text on the old one;
a getter slot (`{() => i18n.dict.title}`) reads the new one. A binding that throws while refreshing is
reported as `MJX208` and the remaining ones still run.

Only what is in the component's binding registry is refreshed. A free `effect()` created in a component is not
in it: `setState()` / `reState()` never re-run it, even when its stop function is registered with
`motif.setDisposable` (that only stops it on dispose). Work that must follow plain data after a refresh is
written as a binding or with `bindings.watch`, not as a free effect.

## The list-scan trap (n² dependencies)

A row that holds only an id and finds its item in a getter, `{() => notes.items.find((n) => n.id === props.id)?.title}`,
subscribes to the `id` of every item it passes: n dependencies for one row, n² for n rows. An id change reruns every row
that scanned past it and a list replacement reruns every row, each scanning the list again; a `push` wakes only the rows
that found no match. Measured with 2000 rows over 2000 items: two million subscriptions, 1.2 s to set up, 0.8 s for one id
change, 4 s to replace the list. The scan itself is cheap; the subscriptions are the cost.
`includes`/`indexOf` read no item field and are not affected; "scanning the whole list" (`filter(...).length`) makes it worse.

How it shows: the compiler warns `MJX004` on `find`/`findIndex`/`some`/`every` with an `x.field === value` predicate inside
a reactive getter; at run time `MJX210` fires when two or more instances of one component scan the same reactive list with a
lookup method and the list is at least as long as their count, wherever it came from (props, another module, a service); an effect that tracks
more than 1000 dependencies in one run warns `MJX209`, naming the owner component and binding when devtools are on; the
DevTools inspector lists the dependency count of each effect.

Avoid it, in this order:

1. Hand the row its item, not its id: `{notes.items.map((note) => <NoteRow note={note} />)}`; the row reads
   `props.note.title` and subscribes to that one field.
2. When only an id is available, keep a keyed index in the store and read `byId(id)`: a reactive `Map` subscribes the row
   to its key only, and a change wakes only that key's readers.

   ```ts
   const state = reactive({ items: [] as Note[], byId: new Map<number, Note>() });
   export const notes = {
     get items(): readonly Note[] { return state.items; },
     byId(id: number) { return state.byId.get(id); },
     add(note: Note) { state.items.push(note); state.byId.set(note.id, note); },
     remove(id: number) { const i = state.items.findIndex((n) => n.id === id); if (i >= 0) state.items.splice(i, 1); state.byId.delete(id); },
   };
   ```

   For a list that rarely changes a computed index does: `const index = createComputed(() => new Map(state.items.map((n) => [n.id, n])))`;
   one scan per change, rows read `index.value.get(id)` and rerun once per change with a single read each.
3. When no subscription is wanted, read the list with `untracked(() => notes.items.find(...))`; another dependency has to rerun
   the getter.

## Gotchas

- Reading a reactive field **outside** a getter in `view()` captures a snapshot: `const n = this.state.count; <p>{n}</p>` never updates.
- Destructuring a reactive object (`const { count } = state`) loses reactivity.
- Array mutators (`push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `reverse`) do not track their own internal
  reads, so `state.items.push(x)` inside an effect does not subscribe the effect to the array (an explicit
  read such as `state.items.length` still does). `sort` is not one of them: it reads and writes the array in
  place, so `state.items.sort()` inside an effect retriggers the effect until `MJX203`; sort inside
  `untracked(...)` or sort a copy (`[...state.items].sort()`).
- Array reads subscribe to the array once, not per index: `find`, `findIndex`, `some`, `every`, `filter`, `map`,
  `forEach`, `reduce`, `join`, `slice`, `includes`, `indexOf`, the iterators, `for...of` and spread. A write to an
  index or the length and the structural methods wake the reader once. A lookup that stops at a match (`find`, `findIndex`,
  `some`, `every`, `indexOf`, `includes`) depends only on the prefix it read: a write, an insertion or a `push` beyond the
  index where it stopped does not wake it; a lookup without a match and `findLast`/`findLastIndex` depend on the whole list.
  The fields the callback reads on items (`item.id`) subscribe to those items as well — see *The list-scan trap* above.
- `createComputed` recomputes on the next microtask, so a synchronous read right after a write may see
  the previous value; `createLazyComputed` is marked dirty synchronously and recomputes on read.
- Replacing a whole array (`state.items = newArr`) is fine: rows are matched by item object identity,
  so objects that are in both arrays keep their rows; fresh objects (e.g. a refetched list) get new rows
  even when their `key`/`id` is the same.
- An effect or binding getter that throws is reported as a `MotifError` with code `MJX208` (original
  error in `cause`) to the console and `errorHandler.addListener(fn)` listeners; the other effects in
  the flush keep running. The throwing run produces no value: `effect`'s `onValueChanged` is not called and
  a `when`/`ternary`/`switchCase` branch, like `text`/`attr`/`class`, keeps its last good state. A throwing (or rejected async) event handler is reported as `MJX123`.
- Updates are flushed on a microtask; in tests `await Promise.resolve()` (the local `nextTick()` helper in testing.md; `@motifx/core` exports none) before asserting.

---

<!-- references/conditionals-lists-frames.md -->

# Conditionals, lists, frames and slots

## `x-wait` — the primary way to show/hide (prefer this)

```tsx
<p x-wait={() => !state.loggedIn}>Welcome back</p>     // waits WHILE the fn returns true
<p x-display={() => state.loggedIn}>Welcome back</p>   // exact inverse, same machinery
```
Compiled to `bindings.wait` / `bindings.display`. Works on plain DOM tags, class components (elementless
ones included), function components and Options components alike.

Measured behaviour (`packages/tests/src/components/x-wait-semantics.test.ts`):

- **Lazy build.** If the condition is `true` on first evaluation the element is never `build()`ed —
  neither it nor its subtree enters the DOM, a placeholder is left instead. The component object still
  exists: a class runs its constructor and `onInitializing`/`onInitialized`/`onConfig`/`onConfigured`, a
  function component runs its body; `view()`, `onBuilding`/`onBuilt`/`onMounted` and the subtree's setup
  wait until it first becomes visible. A panel that starts closed builds no view until then.
- **Instance preserved.** After the first build, toggling only hides/shows. The component is **not**
  disposed, so scroll position, form input and third-party plugin state survive. `onDisposing`/
  `onDisposed` do not fire.
- **Both are synchronous on first render.** The first content navigated into an empty `Frame`
  lands during `build()`, so `&&`, ternary and a JSX-returning `{this.part()}` are in the DOM when
  `build()` returns — same as the directive. Later branch *changes* are async (the outgoing content
  is awaited-disposed first; latest navigation wins).

A hidden element leaves the DOM with either strategy: the default puts a `<!--h-->` trace in its place,
`options={{ hideStrategy: 'detach' }}` leaves none and re-inserts by position in the parent. Hiding fires
`onDeactivated` on the component and its visible subtree (`onActivated` when it is shown again); bindings
keep running while hidden, so the element comes back with current values.

## `&&` — only when you actually want construct/dispose

```tsx
{state.loggedIn && <p>Welcome back</p>}
```
Compiled to `bindings.when`. A **new instance is created** every time the condition becomes truthy
and **disposed** every time it becomes falsy. The branch is rebuilt only when the condition **value**
changes (`Object.is`; two falsy values count as the same): `{state.n > 0 && <X/>}` keeps the same `X`
while `n` goes 1 → 2 → 3, and `{state.user && <X/>}` rebuilds when `state.user` is replaced by
another object. A number condition renders nothing for `0` (no `0` text), but
`{state.items.length && <X/>}` rebuilds `X` on every count change; write `> 0` to keep it.

Choose it only when that churn is the point: a third-party plugin that must really be destroyed, or
content too heavy to keep in memory while hidden. Otherwise `x-wait` is cheaper and more predictable.

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Show/hide, state must survive | `x-wait` / `x-display` |
| Starts hidden, heavy content | `x-wait` (never built) |
| Must genuinely dispose on hide | `{cond && <X/>}` |
| One of two branches | ternary |
| Only text changes | getter |

## Ternary

```tsx
{state.loading ? <Spinner /> : <Content data={state.data} />}
{state.level > 2 ? <Gold/> : state.level > 1 ? <Silver/> : <Bronze/>}   // nested OK
```
Compiled to `bindings.ternary`; each branch receives a `Frame` and `navigate()`s into it. The old
branch's running animations are cancelled, then it is disposed and **plays its leave transition** if it
has one; the new branch is placed at once and the order follows the nearest element ancestor's
transition `mode` (`concurrent` default, `out-in`, `in-out` — `<div transition={{ mode: 'out-in' }}>`
around the expression works). The same holds for `&&`, `{this.method()}`, `switch` swaps and every
`frame.navigate`. Without a leave transition the new branch is placed after the old one has finished
disposing. A branch is rebuilt only when its condition value changes (`Object.is`); in a nested ternary
the inner branch is kept while the outer value stays the same.

**Props inside a branch are snapshots.** The branch is built once and kept while the condition value
stays the same, so a component prop written as a plain expression (`<Content data={state.data} />`,
`<Badge count={state.n} />`) holds the value from when the branch was built, exactly as outside a
conditional. Pass a getter and read it with the `Bind<T>` contract to keep it live:

```tsx
<Badge count={() => state.n} />
// Badge: interface Props { count: Bind<number> }  …  <span>{() => read(this.props.count)}</span>
```

For plain text use a getter instead: `<span>{() => state.done ? '✓' : '✗'}</span>`. It compiles to
`bindings.ternary` with a text node per branch; the hand-written single binding is `bindings.text(fn)`,
which sets the element's `textContent` and so removes any other children.

### Compiler restriction (important)

Inside a JSX child position, **do not** write a block-bodied arrow that declares locals and then
returns a conditional:

```tsx
{() => { const label = compute(state.x); return state.ok ? <A t={label}/> : <B/>; }}  // ✗ ReferenceError: label
```
The compiler lifts the conditional out of the closure. Use an expression-bodied arrow, move the
logic into a named method, or compute inside the branch:

```tsx
{() => state.ok ? <A t={compute(state.x)}/> : <B/>}                                   // ✓
{this.renderStatus()}   // where renderStatus() returns bindings-free JSX or a component  // ✓
```

## Lists with `.map`

```tsx
const state = reactive({ todos: [{ id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false }] });

<ul>
  {state.todos.map(todo => (
    <li key={todo.id} class={() => todo.done ? 'done' : ''}>
      <input type="checkbox" checked={() => todo.done} onchange={(e) => todo.done = e.target.checked} />
      {todo.title}
      <button onclick={() => state.todos.splice(state.todos.indexOf(todo), 1)}>×</button>
    </li>
  ))}
</ul>
```

- Compiled to `bindings.list(() => state.todos, (todo) => ...)`. Add/remove/reorder patch the
  DOM minimally (identity diff with longest-increasing-subsequence moves).
- **Row identity is the item object** (the raw object behind the proxy), not `key`: an object present
  in the old and new array keeps its row (moved if needed); a removed object's row is disposed; fresh
  objects (a refetched list) get new rows even with the same `id`. The same object may appear more
  than once (`push(items[0])`, `splice(i, 0, items[j])`): each occurrence gets its own row, all
  showing that object. Array methods never copy items; write `{ ...item }` for an independent copy.
  Primitive items (`string[]`) keep
  their row when the same value stays at the same index, or anywhere when the render function takes
  no `index` parameter. An object item's row is reused when it moves, so the `index` a render function
  receives is the position when the row was built; a sort does not update it.
- **`key`**: still give a stable unique value; it identifies items. It does not take part in matching
  and does not change DOM reuse; a duplicate key raises the `MJX202` dev warning, and a `.map` without
  `key` raises the compiler warning `MJX003`.
- Items are reactive: mutating `todo.done` updates only that row.
- `{state.todos.filter(t => !t.done).map(...)}` is reactive when the filter reads reactive fields.
- `items.map(function (item) { … }, ctx)`: the second `map` argument is honoured as `this`.
- The render function must return a component (instance, class or factory); anything else throws
  `MJX201` (reported through the list effect as `MJX208`) and that update places no rows at all. To
  skip items, filter first (`.filter(...).map(...)`) instead of returning `null`.
- **Thousands of rows in one update block the page while they build.** Put `x-chunk` on the
  element that holds the rows: the first 100 build at once, the rest are created in order over the
  next frames, each with the index it has when its turn comes; an item removed before its turn never
  gets a row. Each frame builds as many as keep the frame (building plus the browser's layout) near
  50 ms. `x-chunk={50}` builds exactly 50 at once and at least 50 per frame. Rows are created lazily
  only for a bare `{items.map(...)}`; inside a getter `{() => items.map(...)}` every row component
  is created up front and only their builds are sliced. The browser relays out the whole container
  every frame, a table most of all, so past roughly 10–30 thousand table rows (a few tens of thousands
  of plain rows) frames grow long. The DOM still ends up holding every row — when it should not, use
  `Virtualization` (`references/virtualization.md`).

## `switch`-like rendering

```ts
this.bindings.switchCase(
  () => state.status,
  {
    loading: (frame) => frame.navigate(<Spinner />),
    ready:   (frame) => frame.navigate(<Content />),
    error:   (frame) => frame.navigate(<ErrorView />),
  },
  (frame) => frame.navigate(<Empty />)   // default, optional
);
```

In JSX write a `switch` inside a block-bodied getter; the compiler turns the `case` branches into
`switchCase`:

```tsx
<div>
  {() => {
    switch (state.status) {
      case 'loading': return <Spinner />;
      case 'ready':   return <Content />;
      default:        return <Empty />;
    }
  }}
</div>
```
`case` labels must be string, number or boolean **literals**. Statements before the `switch` run in
the discriminant getter on every evaluation and the branches see those locals (read when the branch is
built, so they do not update it while the discriminant stays the same); statements before a
`return` inside a case run when the branch is built; fall-through (`case 'a': case 'b': return <X/>;`)
shows `X` for `'a'` too; a branch leaving with `break` and the statements after the `switch` run on the
default path. A branch returning `null` or `undefined` (`default: return null`, `return ok ? <X/> : null`)
empties the slot. Moving from one unmatched value to another keeps the default branch. In a
hand-written `switchCase`, `frame.navigate(null)` places nothing and leaves the previous content; empty
the slot with `frame.flush()`. A shape the compiler cannot lower (a non-literal or repeated `case`
label, a second `default` or `switch`, a `return`, JSX-creating statement or class declaration before
the `switch`, a `break`/`continue` that is labeled or not the last statement of its case) runs as
written through `bindings.method` and the compiler warns `MJX016`: no branch is kept, the content is
rebuilt on every change. The same holds for `{() => { const x = …; return c ? <A/> : <B/>; }}`:
the locals are kept and the condition getter runs them.

## `Frame` — a slot you navigate programmatically

```tsx
import { Frame } from '@motifx/core';

class Shell extends Component<HTMLDivElement> {
  frame = new Frame();
  view() { return <><nav/>{this.frame}</>; }
  async showSettings() { await this.frame.navigate(<Settings />); }   // disposes previous content
  async showLazy() { await this.frame.navigateLazy(() => import('./Reports'), { Loaderview: new Spinner() }); }
}
```

`frame.navigate(component | component[], keepOldControl = false)`, `frame.flush()`, `frame.motif.clear()`,
`frame.current`, `frame.isBusy`. Navigation is serialised and "latest wins".

- Navigating to the component that is already `frame.current` (or to `null`) does nothing.
- A `Promise` (e.g. `import('./Reports')`) is also accepted at runtime and wrapped in `Lazy`; the
  parameter is typed as a component, so cast it. `navigateLazy` is the typed form.
- `keepOldControl = true` keeps the previous content instead of disposing it.
- `frame.flush()` disposes the current content (playing its leave transition) without navigating;
  `frame.current` still references the disposed content.

## `Lazy` — dynamic import as a component

```tsx
import { Lazy } from '@motifx/core';

<Lazy caller={() => import('./HeavyChart')}
      options={{ Loaderview: new Spinner(), Fallbackview: new ErrorBox(), minDelayMs: 200, timeoutMs: 10000 }} />
```
`LazyOptions`: `Loaderview`, `Placeholderview`, `Fallbackview`, `minDelayMs`, `timeoutMs`, `signal`,
`onError`, `mapResult` (default: `module.default` when it is a function, otherwise the whole resolved
value), `retry` (count or `{ count, delayMs?, whenOnline? }`),
`onRetry(attempt, error)`. On failure `onError(err)` runs first; then `Fallbackview` is shown if set,
otherwise the host is cleared and the failure is reported as `MJX126` (`errorHandler.report`, original
error in `cause`). An aborted load is never reported.

## `Transport` / `TransportTo` — portal-style slots

```tsx
// somewhere in the layout
<Transport name="toolbar" mode="replace" />      // or mode="merge"

// in any page
<TransportTo name="toolbar"><button>Save</button></TransportTo>
```
Children of `TransportTo` are moved into the `Transport` slot with the same name and removed (and
disposed) when the `TransportTo` is disposed; their bindings keep working against the sender's state.
When the sender is a route page that is left, they leave the slot at once, before the page is disposed.
Order does not matter: a `TransportTo` built before its slot delivers when the slot registers.
`TransportTo` itself leaves an empty `<div>` in place. Children added later to the `TransportTo`'s
`controls` go straight to the slot, stay alive there and are disposed with the sender like the initial
children. When the slot is disposed its transported content is disposed too.
Several senders on one slot: `mode="replace"` (default) keeps only the most recently built sender's
content (the previous content is disposed and does not come back), `mode="merge"` appends every
sender's content in build order and removes each sender's own content when it closes. Needs a
running `Application` (the pair talks over application events).

`transport.clearSlot()` removes and disposes everything currently in a `Transport` slot.

`ContentBody name="x"` / `ContentBlock target="x"` is a simpler slot pair without modes; prefer
`Transport`.

## Showing/hiding without recreating

```tsx
<div x-display={() => state.open} options={{ hideStrategy: 'detach' }}>Heavy panel</div>
```
`x-display` toggles visibility (with transitions) instead of disposing; use `&&` when you want
the subtree destroyed. `hideStrategy` is given through the `options` prop (or set on `motif.options` in code): `'placeholder'`
(a `<!--h-->` comment trace stays in place), `'detach'` (node removed without a trace), `'auto'` (default,
same as `'placeholder'`). Every hidden or waiting component keeps a trace, list rows and components that wait from
the start included; `controls.move` and list reordering carry the trace with the component. On a plain DOM tag `options` writes no attribute.

---

<!-- references/events-and-forms.md -->

# Events and forms

## DOM events in JSX

```tsx
<button onclick={() => save()}>Save</button>
<input oninput={(e) => state.q = (e.target as HTMLInputElement).value} />
<form onsubmit={(sender, e) => { e.preventDefault(); submit(); }}>…</form>
<a href="/home" onclick:prevent={(s, e) => s.context.navigate('/home')}>Home</a>
```

- Names are lowercase DOM names (`onclick`, `onchange`, `onkeydown`, `onpointerdown`). On a plain tag any
  DOM event binds this way, and a camelCase spelling (`onClick`) binds the same event.
- On a **component tag**, a prop named like a DOM event (`onchange`/`onChange`, `onCopy`, `onResize`,
  `onSelect`, `onReset`, `onContextMenu` …) is bound as a DOM listener on the component's own element and
  never reaches `this.props` (the compiler warns `MJX002` for the camelCase spelling). On a fragment
  component (no element) the listener listens on the content elements: every top-level child element, nested fragments included, later children too; `:self`, `:once` and `off` cover all of them. Name callback props
  so they do not collide: `onValueChange`, `onConfirm`. A name the compiler does not know as a DOM event
  (`onmouseenter`, `onpointer…`, `ontouch…`, `onfocusin`, `onanimation…`, `ontransition…`) creates no listener
  on a component tag: the value passes as an ordinary prop, without a warning. Listen to such an event on the
  component's element with `on:mouseenter={…}`; a lowercase known name (`<Button onclick={…}>`) is a
  deliberate DOM listener and does not warn.
- A ternary in a handler position (`onclick={a ? save : edit}`, `on:click`, `onclick:once`, also on a
  component tag) runs no handler: the compiler wraps it in a getter, the getter becomes the listener and the
  handler it returns is not called, with no warning. Put the condition inside the handler:
  `onclick={() => (a ? save() : edit())}`.
- A handler that throws, or an async handler whose promise rejects, is reported as `MotifError` `MJX123`
  (`The '<event>' event handler threw.`, original error in `cause`) through `errorHandler`: logged to the
  console in production too (`app.useLogging(false)` turns it off) and delivered to
  `errorHandler.addListener(fn)`. Other listeners of the event still run.
- Handler arity decides the signature: 1 param → `(event)`, 2 params → `(sender, event)` where
  `sender` is the `ComponentBase` (`sender.element`, `sender.context`, `sender.props`).
- Under `strict` both forms are typed from the element's event on plain and component tags
  (`onkeydown={(e) => e.key}` → `KeyboardEvent`); no annotation is needed. Modifier props take the
  same type as the unmodified event (`onkeydown:once={(e) => e.key}`). The first parameter is typed
  `Event & ComponentBase` because its meaning depends on arity: use event members in `(e) => …`,
  component members in `(s, e) => …`.
- Returning `{ cancel: true }` → `preventDefault()` + `stopPropagation()`. Every other return value,
  `false` included, is ignored: `onkeydown={(e) => e.key === 'Enter' && submit()}` leaves other keys
  alone. To cancel use `:prevent` / `:stop`, `e.preventDefault()` or `{ cancel: true }`. These (and the
  `:prevent` / `:stop` modifiers) are called only when the event object has them: with
  `motif.trigger('name', { … })` and a plain data object nothing is called and no error is raised.
- Listeners are removed automatically on dispose.
- Arity is `fn.length`, which stops at the first default-valued or rest parameter: `(...a) => …`
  counts 0 and receives only the event.

### `on:name` / `on-name` / `on_name`

This spelling binds the handler as is to the tag's component: `<X on:save={fn}/>` is
`sender.motif.on('save', fn)`. Only the prefix is stripped: `on-my-event` → `my-event`,
`on_my_event` → `my_event`. It works for DOM events and for custom events fired with
`motif.trigger`, with the same arity rule (1 param → `fn(event)`, 2+ → `fn(sender, event)`).
The name is free-form, so the parameters are typed `any`; give the data its type in the parameter
(`on:saved={(saved: Note) => …}`).

```tsx
<Editor on:save={(e) => console.log(e.id)} />      // Editor: this.motif.trigger('save', { id: 7 })
<button on-click={(s, e) => s.motif.hide()}>Close</button>
```

### Modifiers (append with `:`)

`once`, `prevent`, `stop`, `capture`, `passive`, `self` (only when `event.target === element`),
`trusted` (only `isTrusted`). A JSX attribute takes one modifier (`onclick:once`, `onscroll:passive`; JSX syntax allows a single `:`);
chains such as `click:once:prevent` are written with the imperative API below. `:once` holds for every path: a DOM dispatch or a `motif.trigger('click:once', …)` runs the handler one time and removes it (`hasEvent` turns `false`).

## Imperative event API

The imperative API lives on the `this.motif` namespace (a subclass may define its own `on`/`off`/`trigger` methods).

```ts
this.motif.on('click', (s, e) => …);         // returns Promise<this>; auto-removed on dispose
this.motif.on('click:once:prevent', handler);
this.motif.on('x:mounted', () => …);         // once per subscription, in a later task after the element reaches document (also when it is already there); NOT again on re-attach — use x:activated; motif.off('x:mounted', fn) cancels a pending one
this.motif.on('x:built', (sender, e) => …); // lifecycle events via the x: prefix: initializing, initialized, config, configured, building, built, mounted, visibilityChanged, activated, deactivated, disposing, disposed; motif.off(name, fn) removes every subscription of fn; initializing and initialized are over when the constructor returns, so a later subscription runs the handler once right away; a throwing x: listener (x:mounted included) is reported as MJX122 ("The component x:built hook threw.")
this.motif.on('custom-thing', handler, false); // 3rd arg false = internal event only (no addEventListener)
this.motif.trigger('custom-thing', { data: 1 }); // fire internal/custom event
this.motif.off('click', handler);
this.motif.addHandler('click', handler);     // same as motif.on(event, handler)
this.motif.toggle();                          // hide when visible, show otherwise
```

- Handlers are stored under the full lowercased event string, modifiers included. `trigger('save')` does
  not reach a handler registered as `'save:once'`, and `off('click', fn)` does not remove
  `on('click:once', fn)`; pass the same string to `off`.
- `trigger(name, data)` calls the stored handlers directly (DOM listeners registered through `on` for
  that name included); it dispatches no DOM event.
- `off` for a DOM/custom event removes only the first record matching `fn`; a handler registered twice
  needs two `off` calls. For `x:` lifecycle names `off` removes every subscription of `fn`.

## Application-wide event bus

```ts
const off = this.context.on('languageChanged', (payload) => …);   // returns unsubscribe fn
this.context.fire('languageChanged', { lang: 'en' });
this.context.off('languageChanged', handler);
this.context.onRouterChanged((ctx) => …);                          // every navigation, incl. initial + 404
off();                                                             // optional: leave early
```

`this.context` is a component-scoped view of the application: subscriptions opened through its `on`
and `onRouterChanged` are removed automatically when the component is disposed, so nothing has to be
registered. Subscriptions opened on `Application.main`, a captured `app` or
`useApplication().application` are not tied to a component; register their unsubscribe with
`this.motif.setDisposable(off)` or call it yourself.

A listener that throws (`app.on` / `app.fire`, `onRouterChanged` included) is reported as `MJX123`
(`The 'motifjs-router-navigated' event handler threw.` for `onRouterChanged`); the other listeners
still run and the navigation completes.

## Forms

### One-way + event (explicit, preferred when validating/transforming)

```tsx
const f = reactive({ email: '', agree: false, lang: 'en', note: '' });

<form onsubmit:prevent={() => submit(f)}>
  <input type="email" value={() => f.email} oninput={(e) => f.email = e.target.value} />
  <input type="checkbox" checked={() => f.agree} onchange={(e) => f.agree = e.target.checked} />
  <select value={() => f.lang} onchange={(e) => f.lang = e.target.value}>
    <option value="en">English</option><option value="tr">Türkçe</option>
  </select>
  <textarea value={() => f.note} oninput={(e) => f.note = e.target.value} />
  <button type="submit" disabled={() => !f.agree}>Send</button>
</form>
```

### Two-way with `x-model` / `bindings.model`

```tsx
<input type="text"     x-model={() => f.email} />
<input type="checkbox" x-model={() => f.agree} />
<input type="text"     onConfig={(s) => s.bindings.model(f, 'email')} />
```
`x-model` takes a getter (or a bare member expression, `x-model={f.email}`) and compiles to
`bindings.model(getter, setter)`. The setter reads the owner again on every write (`f` in `f.email`,
`row` in `row.name`, `s.form` in `s.form.name`), so the binding keeps working when the owner object is
replaced (`s.form = {…}`) and when list rows are reordered. The write is skipped while the owner is
`null`/`undefined` (`x-model={() => s.current?.name}`) and when the member holds a function (a getter
prop is never overwritten). A value that is not a member access (`() => a + b`, `() => fn(x)`, a plain
identifier, a `function` expression, a block body with more than one statement) gets no setter and binds
one-way; `motif-explain` reports which case applies.

`model` picks the DOM property by element type: checkbox/radio → `checked` (boolean); number/range →
number (`null` when empty); other inputs, select, textarea → `value`; img/audio/video → `src` (one-way,
nothing is written back). Signatures: `model(getter, setter)`, `model(source, member)`,
